questions.question: How do you set up a Spring WebFlux application with controllers, routing, and WebClient?
questions.title: Spring WebFlux Setup — Controllers, Functional Routing, WebClient
questions.direct_answer: A WebFlux application uses **`spring-boot-starter-webflux`**, which brings Reactor plus **Netty** by default. You write endpoints as **annotated controllers** (`@RestController` returning `Mono` / `Flux`) or via **functional routing** (`RouterFunction` + `HandlerFunction`). For outbound calls, use **`WebClient`** — never `RestTemplate` — with explicit timeouts, connection pool tuning, and retry. Add cross-cutting concerns via `WebFilter`, secure with `@EnableWebFluxSecurity`, configure CORS via `CorsWebFilter`, serve SSE by returning `Flux<ServerSentEvent<T>>`, and test with `WebTestClient` plus `StepVerifier`. Never block on the event-loop thread; wrap any blocking call in `Schedulers.boundedElastic()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical setup, awareness of annotated vs functional styles, WebClient hygiene, and observability hooks
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using RestTemplate in WebFlux; default WebClient without timeouts or pool config; mixing blocking libraries on the event loop

sections.title: WebFlux at a Glance
sections.content:
Spring WebFlux is the reactive counterpart to Spring MVC. The same `@RestController` / `@RequestMapping` annotations work, but return types are `Mono<T>` / `Flux<T>` and the underlying server is non-blocking — Netty by default.

**What you get by adding `spring-boot-starter-webflux`:**
- Reactor Netty server (Undertow / Jetty reactive available as alternatives)
- Reactor Core — `Mono` and `Flux`
- `WebClient` reactive HTTP client
- Annotation-based controllers and functional routing
- Server-Sent Events and WebSocket support
- Reactive `@Valid`, content negotiation, Jackson codecs, WebFlux-native security

**Two programming styles**
- **Annotated controllers** — same look as MVC; quickest to onboard
- **Functional routing** — `RouterFunction` + `HandlerFunction`; explicit and composable, often used for gateways and small services

**Reactive ecosystem you'll likely need:**
- `spring-boot-starter-data-r2dbc` — reactive relational
- `spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb-reactive`
- `spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive`
- Reactor Kafka
- Spring Security with `@EnableWebFluxSecurity`
- Spring Cloud Gateway (built on WebFlux)

sections.title: Annotated Controllers
Functional Routing
WebClient — Outbound Calls Done Right
WebFilter, Security, CORS, Testing
Common Gotchas, Deployment, and Starter Checklist
sections.content:
**Common gotchas:**
- **Don't use `RestTemplate` in WebFlux** — it blocks the event loop
- **Don't use blocking JDBC without `boundedElastic`** — wrap with `Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic())`
- **Default Netty event-loop thread count** is `CPU cores × 2`; rarely tune
- **Connection pool per upstream** — never share one `WebClient` with different configs
- **`@RequestBody Foo` vs `@RequestBody Mono<Foo>`** — the latter streams; the former materializes; both are fine, choose based on payload size
- **CORS** uses `CorsWebFilter`, not `CorsFilter`
- **Session and cookies** use the reactive `WebSession`
- **Exception handling** uses `@ControllerAdvice` with reactive exception handlers (see error-handling topic)
- **Never `.block()` in the request handling path** — deadlock or stall risk
- **Observability** — Spring Boot auto-wires Micrometer (`http.server.requests`) and OpenTelemetry tracing

**Packaging and deployment:**
- Executable jar (`mvn package`); run with `java -jar`
- Netty is lightweight; cold-start similar to MVC
- Container — use `eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine` base; set `-Xmx` and `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`
- Readiness probe — `/actuator/health/readiness`; liveness — `/actuator/health/liveness`
- Observability — expose `/actuator/prometheus` and an OpenTelemetry exporter

**Starter checklist:**
- Replace all `RestTemplate` with `WebClient`
- Configure `WebClient` pool and timeouts per upstream
- Use R2DBC or wrap JDBC with `boundedElastic`
- Global `@RestControllerAdvice` for errors
- `WebFilter` for tracing / request ID
- Security with `@EnableWebFluxSecurity`
- Test with `WebTestClient` and `StepVerifier`
- Actuator endpoints with readiness / liveness probes
- Enable BlockHound in tests to catch accidental blocking

**Strategic guidance:**
- Annotated controllers are the right default for most teams
- Functional routing pays off for API gateways or small composable services
- The `WebClient` configuration is where most production bugs hide — invest there
- Observability is auto-wired but you must expose and watch it
- BlockHound in CI is the cheapest insurance against the worst class of WebFlux bugs

sections.content:

- **Return `Mono<T>` / `Flux<T>`** from handlers; Spring subscribes automatically
- **SSE** — return `Flux<ServerSentEvent<T>>` with `produces = TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE`
- **Functional routing** (`RouterFunction`) for explicit composable routes
- **Use `WebClient`, never `RestTemplate`** — one client per upstream with pool, timeouts, retries

- **Reactive security** via `@EnableWebFluxSecurity` and `SecurityWebFilterChain`
- **Reactive CORS** — `CorsWebFilter` (not `CorsFilter`)
- **Test with `WebTestClient` and `StepVerifier`**

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
WebFlux is the reactive counterpart to Spring MVC. Add `spring-boot-starter-webflux` and you get Reactor plus Netty by default.

**Two styles**
- Annotated controllers — `@RestController` returning `Mono` / `Flux`; quickest to onboard
- Functional routing — `RouterFunction` + `HandlerFunction`; explicit and composable; good for gateways

**Endpoint notes**
- `switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(NotFoundException))` is the idiomatic 404
- SSE — `Flux<ServerSentEvent<T>>` with `produces = TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE`
- `@Valid @RequestBody Mono<Foo>` for reactive validation

**WebClient — outbound done right**
- Always `WebClient`, never `RestTemplate`
- One bean per upstream — separate pools, timeouts, retries
- `responseTimeout`, connect timeout, read / write timeout
- `onStatus` for 4xx / 5xx mapping
- `retryWhen(Retry.backoff(...))` filtered to retryable errors
- Circuit breaker via Resilience4j

**WebFilter for cross-cutting**
- Implements `WebFilter`; use `Context.of` to propagate trace IDs into the reactive chain
- `@Order` controls execution
- For security, prefer `SecurityWebFilterChain`

**Security**
- `@EnableWebFluxSecurity` and `SecurityWebFilterChain`
- `authorizeExchange` with path matchers
- `oauth2ResourceServer.jwt` for JWT

**CORS**
- `CorsWebFilter`, not `CorsFilter`

**Testing**
- `WebTestClient` with `@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)`
- `StepVerifier` for reactive streams
- BlockHound in tests catches accidental blocking

**Common gotchas**
- `RestTemplate` in WebFlux blocks the event loop
- Blocking JDBC needs `Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(boundedElastic())`
- One `WebClient` per upstream; never share with different configs
- CORS is `CorsWebFilter` not `CorsFilter`
- Never `.block()` in the handler path

**Deployment**
- Executable jar; `java -jar`
- Container with `eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine`
- Readiness / liveness probes via Actuator
- Prometheus and OpenTelemetry exporters

**Strategic answer**
- Annotated controllers for most teams; functional routing for gateways
- WebClient configuration is where most production bugs hide — invest there
- Observability is auto-wired but must be exposed and watched
- BlockHound in CI is cheap insurance

questions.question: WebFlux vs Spring MVC — how do you choose between thread-per-request and event-loop?
questions.title: WebFlux vs MVC Stack Choice — Thread-per-Request vs Event Loop
questions.direct_answer: **Spring MVC** is the classic blocking, **thread-per-request** stack on Tomcat / Jetty / Undertow — simple, mature, JDBC-friendly. **Spring WebFlux** is the **event-loop** stack on Netty — handful of threads serve thousands of in-flight calls; native streaming (SSE / WebSocket) and explicit backpressure. The choice in 2026 is between three stacks: classic MVC (older code), MVC + virtual threads (default for new services), and WebFlux (streaming, reactive-all-the-way). Pick WebFlux when streaming, RSocket, or true reactive composition is the requirement; pick MVC + virtual threads for everything else. The deciding factor is rarely raw throughput — it's whether your downstream stack is reactive end-to-end and whether your team can absorb the debugging cost.

sections.title: Three Stacks, One Decision
sections.content:
Spring offers three real options for HTTP services in 2026, and the right default has shifted with virtual threads.

**Spring MVC (classic)** is the servlet stack on Tomcat / Jetty / Undertow. Each request is served by one OS thread that blocks on I/O. The thread pool (typically 200) is the concurrency limit. JDBC, JPA, `RestTemplate`, normal stack traces, mature tooling.

**Spring WebFlux (reactive)** is the Netty event-loop stack. A handful of event-loop threads handle thousands of in-flight requests. Endpoints return `Mono<T>` / `Flux<T>`; outbound calls use `WebClient`; databases use R2DBC. Native streaming (SSE / WebSocket); explicit backpressure built in.

**Spring MVC + Virtual Threads (Boot 3.2+, JDK 21)** runs the regular MVC servlet stack on Project Loom virtual threads.
- Set `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true` and each request runs on a virtual thread — blocking I/O parks the virtual thread without blocking its carrier.
- Thousands of concurrent requests scale on a handful of carriers while your code remains plain blocking Java.

**The 2024-2026 shift** — virtual threads let blocking code reach reactive-like concurrency.
- For most services in 2026, MVC + virtual threads is the right default.
- WebFlux earns its place for specific reasons — streaming, reactive-all-the-way, RSocket, explicit backpressure — not as a universal scaling answer.

```mermaid
        vthread --> ctl3["Controller blocks on JDBC"]
        vthread -.park.-> carrier["~8 carrier threads"]
        ctl3 --> db2[(Database)]
    end
```

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
Each stack makes a different bet across the same dimensions. Programming model, threads, and library compatibility are usually the deciding rows.

| Dimension | Spring MVC | WebFlux | MVC + Virtual Threads |
|---|---|---|---|
| Programming model | Blocking, imperative | Reactive (Mono/Flux) | Blocking, imperative |
| Server | Tomcat / Jetty / Undertow | Netty (default) | Tomcat / Jetty / Undertow |
| Threads | ~200 per instance | 4-8 event-loop | Unlimited virtual; ~8 carrier |
| DB driver | JDBC (blocking) | R2DBC (reactive) | JDBC (virtual-thread friendly) |
| HTTP client | RestTemplate / WebClient / RestClient | WebClient | RestClient / WebClient |
| Streaming (SSE/WS) | Possible but awkward | Excellent, native | OK; not best-in-class |
| Backpressure | None in-process | Explicit | None in-process |
| Learning curve | Low | High | Low |
| Debugging | Normal stack traces | Hard; use checkpoint | Normal |
| MDC / ThreadLocal | Native | Needs Context Propagation | Native (with care) |
| `@Transactional` | Works | Needs reactive tx manager | Works |
| Library compatibility | Universal | Reactive-only matters | Universal |
| Best for | CRUD, REST | Streaming, reactive-all-the-way | Most modern services |

sections.title: When to Pick Each
sections.content:
**Default to MVC + Virtual Threads when:**
- New service on JDK 21+ and Boot 3.2+
- Team familiar with blocking / imperative style
- JDBC or JPA backend
- REST endpoints with moderate streaming needs
- CRUD, CQRS, or standard microservice
- Existing blocking dependencies you can't replace

**Pick Spring WebFlux when:**
- **Streaming is core** — SSE, WebSocket, chunked HTTP streaming
- **Reactive-all-the-way stack** — R2DBC, reactive Kafka, reactive Redis
- **Explicit backpressure** is a genuine requirement (telemetry ingestion, financial ticker)
- **API-gateway-like workloads** composing many HTTP calls asynchronously
- **RSocket** services
- **Memory-critical** environments (small containers, extreme connection counts) where reactive's per-connection efficiency matters
- **Team is experienced with Reactor**

**Stick with classic Spring MVC when:**
- Older JDK (pre-21)
- Older Boot (pre-3.2)
- Moderate load; thread-per-request sufficient
- Maximum library compatibility and zero experimentation risk

**Avoid WebFlux when:**
- Team lacks reactive experience (6+ months of learning curve is real)
- Heavy blocking dependencies you can't replace (wrapping in `boundedElastic` removes the benefit)
- Primarily CPU-bound workloads (reactive doesn't help)
- Service is already healthy on MVC with headroom

**Migration paths**
- **MVC → MVC + virtual threads** — one line of config (`spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`), upgrade JDK, test; low risk
- **MVC → WebFlux** — large effort; rewrite controllers, replace JDBC with R2DBC, retrain team
- **WebFlux → MVC + virtual threads** — common in 2024-2026 when teams realize WebFlux was premature; mostly incremental

sections.title: Honest Pros, Cons, and the Pitfalls of Each
sections.content:
**Spring MVC (classic):**
- **Pros** — simple, familiar, universal library compatibility, mature tooling, normal debugging
- **Cons** — thread-per-request caps concurrency around the pool size; memory cost per connection at scale
- **Sweet spot** — everything that isn't at extreme concurrency

**Spring WebFlux:**
- **Pros** — massive concurrency on few threads; native streaming; explicit backpressure; memory-efficient per connection
- **Cons** — steep learning curve; hard debugging; requires reactive-all-the-way for full benefit; mixing blocking and reactive is the worst case; `@Transactional` complications
- **Sweet spot** — streaming services, reactive API gateways, event-driven systems with truly reactive stacks

**Spring MVC + Virtual Threads:**
- **Pros** — blocking-code simplicity with reactive-like concurrency; normal stack traces; full library compatibility; one-line migration
- **Cons** — pinning with `synchronized` plus blocking I/O; DB pool becomes the bottleneck; tooling still catching up; extreme-scale (100K+) needs tuning
- **Sweet spot** — most modern services in 2026

**Pitfalls to avoid:**
- **Choosing WebFlux "for performance"** without measuring or considering team velocity
- **Mixing WebFlux with blocking JDBC** without `boundedElastic` — stalls the event loop
- **Staying on WebFlux** when team velocity is suffering — migrating back is valid
- **Not upgrading to virtual threads** when the migration is trivial and the wins are real
- **Premature optimization** — picking the hardest stack for a CRUD service
- **Wrong DB pool size with virtual threads** — virtual threads are free but DB connections aren't; the pool becomes the real concurrency limit

**Performance reality check**
- WebFlux slightly edges MVC + virtual threads on pure I/O throughput at extreme concurrency (50K+ connections)
- MVC + virtual threads wins on debugging, developer velocity, and library compatibility
- The gap is usually 10-20%, not orders of magnitude
- Unless you operate at scale where 10% matters (very few services do), simpler wins

**Industry trend in 2026**
- The reactive narrative has shifted
- Reactive is no longer the default answer to "we need scale"
- Virtual threads cover the common case
- Reactive earns its place for specific problems — streaming, backpressure, truly async composition — not universally

**The 2026 decision flowchart** 1.
- Need SSE / WebSocket streaming with backpressure? → WebFlux
2.
- Truly reactive-all-the-way stack (R2DBC, reactive Kafka, Redis)? → WebFlux
3.
- Team is already expert in Reactor? → WebFlux
4.
- Everything else on JDK 21+ / Boot 3.2+? → **MVC + virtual threads**
5.
- Older JDK / Boot, moderate scale? → Classic MVC

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Three stacks** — Spring MVC (blocking), WebFlux (reactive), MVC + Virtual Threads (Loom)
- **MVC + Virtual Threads** is the 2026 default for most new services
- **WebFlux** for streaming (SSE/WS), reactive-all-the-way, explicit backpressure, RSocket
- **Classic MVC** still fine for older JDK or moderate scale
- **Don't mix blocking JDBC with WebFlux** without `boundedElastic`
- **Migration MVC → MVC+VT** is one line of config — low risk
- **Performance gap WebFlux vs MVC+VT** is roughly 10-20% — usually not worth the complexity
- **Virtual thread caveats** — pinning with `synchronized`, DB pool bottleneck, thread-local cost
- **WebFlux caveats** — steep learning curve, debugging hard, needs all-reactive dependencies
- **Streaming, reactive downstream, true async composition = WebFlux; everything else = MVC+VT**

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring offers three real options in 2026, and the default has shifted with virtual threads.

**Spring MVC classic**
- Servlet-based on Tomcat / Jetty / Undertow
- Thread-per-request blocking; ~200 threads per instance
- JDBC, JPA, `RestTemplate`, normal stack traces, mature tooling

**Spring WebFlux reactive**
- Netty-based non-blocking; few event-loop threads handle thousands of connections
- Returns `Mono<T>` / `Flux<T>`; Reactor operators compose
- `WebClient`, R2DBC, reactive Mongo / Redis
- Explicit backpressure; native streaming (SSE, WebSocket); RSocket

**Spring MVC + Virtual Threads (Boot 3.2+, JDK 21)**
- Regular MVC servlet stack with `spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true`
- Each request runs on a virtual thread; blocking I/O parks without blocking the carrier
- Code stays plain blocking Java; `JdbcTemplate.query` just works; stack traces normal

**The shift**
- Virtual threads let blocking code reach reactive-like concurrency
- For most services in 2026, MVC + virtual threads is the right default
- WebFlux earns its place for specific reasons — streaming, RSocket, backpressure, reactive-all-the-way — not as a universal scaling answer

**Decision framework**
- Streaming or reactive-all-the-way → WebFlux
- Everything else on JDK 21+ → MVC + virtual threads
- Older JDK or moderate scale → classic MVC

**Pitfalls**
- Choosing WebFlux "for performance" without measuring
- Mixing WebFlux with blocking JDBC without `boundedElastic`
- Staying on WebFlux when team velocity is suffering
- Not upgrading to virtual threads when migration is trivial

**Performance reality**
- WebFlux slightly edges MVC + virtual threads on extreme concurrency (50K+ connections)
- MVC + virtual threads wins on debugging, velocity, library compatibility
- Gap usually 10-20%, not orders of magnitude

**Strategic answer**
- The reactive narrative has shifted
- Virtual threads cover the common case in 2026
- Reactive earns its place for streaming and explicit backpressure — not universally
- Pick deliberately, not by trend
- Migration MVC → MVC + virtual threads is one line of config; migration MVC → WebFlux is large; migration WebFlux → MVC + virtual threads is increasingly common
